Project Finding Nemo

Search for the better search.

A phased strategy to rebuild trust in search, protect retention and create a controlled path from Apache Solr fundamentals to semantic and AI-assisted discovery.

01
Problem overview

Search is not an isolated feature problem. It is a trust and retention problem.

Users cannot reliably find the assets, campaigns and analytics they need, so the product feels less useful even when the information exists.

User problem

People cannot predict what search will understand.

Inconsistent results, weak metadata and limited intent handling force users to reformulate, browse manually or ask support.

Business problem

Poor findability compounds cost and renewal risk.

Every failed search can become lost time, lower engagement, a support contact or fresh evidence in a difficult renewal conversation.

Strategic problem

The comparison set has moved beyond direct competitors.

Customers now judge enterprise search against fast, conversational and AI-native experiences, raising the minimum bar for relevance and ease.

Decision

Improve the core while earning the right to add AI.

The strategy must create near-term value, preserve governance and generate evidence for larger semantic or generative investment.

02
Problem discovery

Turn three years of complaints into a measurable problem statement.

Use a quick survey to quantify the pattern, then interviews and behavioural data to explain why it occurs.

1

Instrument the search journey.

Track query, result set, first click, refinement, abandonment and downstream task completion as one connected funnel.

2

Segment the failure.

Compare roles, account tiers, content types and known-item versus exploratory tasks so averages do not hide the highest-value pain.

3

Translate friction into business exposure.

Join poor-search cohorts to support hours, product engagement, renewal health and revenue-at-risk rather than claiming direct revenue causality.

4

Sequence stakeholder discovery.

Learn from Customer Success, Support and Analytics first, validate constraints with Engineering and Design, then take evidence to Sales and executives.

Before interviews Five-question search pulse surveyQuantify failure types, starting knowledge, success, workarounds and hardest tasks. About 3 min

1. When search doesn't work the way you expect, what usually goes wrong?

Select all that apply
  • I get no results, even though I think the content exists
  • I get too many irrelevant results
  • The right result exists, but it appears too far down the list
  • I use different words from the words used to name/tag the content
  • The content doesn't have enough useful metadata/tags
  • I find multiple versions and don't know which one is current/correct
  • Content I expect to see doesn't appear because of access/permissions
  • My search is too specific or complicated for search to understand
  • I know roughly what I want, but not exactly what to search for
  • I'm looking for an answer/information rather than a specific asset
  • Search results take too long to load
  • Something else: ______
  • I rarely have problems with search

This is the most valuable survey question because it maps responses directly to the search failure taxonomy.

2. When you're looking for something, what do you usually know about it?

Select all that apply
  • Exact filename or title
  • Part of the filename/title
  • Campaign/project name
  • Brand/product
  • Asset/content type
  • Date or approximate time period
  • Region/market
  • Person/team who created it
  • Tags or metadata
  • Words contained inside the document
  • What the asset looks like
  • I only know roughly what I'm looking for
  • Other: ______

This separates known-item search problems from broader discovery problems.

3. How often do you successfully find what you're looking for using search alone?

Single choice
  • Almost always
  • Most of the time
  • About half the time
  • Occasionally
  • Rarely
  • Never
  • I don't use search enough to say

This creates a simple perceived-success baseline that can be measured again after improvements.

4. What do you normally do when search doesn't find what you need?

Select all that apply
  • Change the words in my search
  • Make the search shorter/simpler
  • Use filters
  • Browse through folders/categories
  • Search using another system/tool
  • Ask a colleague
  • Contact an administrator/support
  • Give up and use something else
  • Create/download another copy because I can't find the original
  • Other: ______

The workaround shows the true cost of failure; asking a colleague or recreating content signals much more pain than a general complaint.

5. Which type of search is hardest for you today?

Single choice
  • Finding a specific asset I know exists
  • Finding the latest/correct version of an asset
  • Finding something when I only remember part of its name
  • Finding something when I don't know how it was named/tagged
  • Finding assets based on what they contain
  • Browsing/discovering content when I don't know exactly what I want
  • Finding information or answers contained within documents
  • Filtering down a large number of results
  • Search generally works well for me
  • Other: ______

This helps distinguish lexical optimisation, semantic retrieval, versioning, metadata and filtering priorities.

Then interview

Use qualitative interviews to explain the patterns behind the survey.

Question 1

Tell me about the last time you needed to find an asset or piece of content. What were you looking for, and how did you go about finding it? Do you use any filters?

This reveals the user's real search workflow, where they begin, and whether they rely on keywords, browsing, filters, or another workaround.

Question 2

What information do you usually know when you start searching?

For example: filename, campaign name, brand, date, asset type, person, tags, or just a rough idea of what you need. These details can become search prefixes or guided prompts, helping users start from what they already know and gradually adopt the terminology the system recognises.

Question 3

Can you think of a recent example where you knew the right asset existed but still couldn't find it? What made it difficult?

This helps identify specific failure modes such as naming differences, missing metadata, weak ranking, unsuitable filters, or access constraints.

Question 4

When you get search results, how do you decide which result is the right one?

This helps uncover important ranking signals like title, thumbnail, date, campaign, owner, approval status, etc.

Question 5

Have you ever searched using synonyms or words that were different from those used to name or tag the asset? What happened?

This is a useful way to uncover a potential semantic-search problem without mentioning "semantic search."

03
Competitive and market analysis

Benchmark the outcomes customers value, not the features vendors advertise.

Compare direct martech competitors, enterprise-search incumbents and AI-native entrants through realistic customer tasks.

01

Relevance and findability

Can users find known items, recover from imperfect queries and see useful results in the first positions?

02

Refinement and control

Are facets, filters, permissions, saved searches and sorting clear enough for high-stakes enterprise work?

03

Semantic and conversational value

Does natural-language or semantic search solve tasks that keyword search misses, or only create an impressive demo?

04

Trust, speed and governance

Are results explainable, permission-safe, current, responsive and grounded in original source material?

The market-noise filter

A competitor feature earns roadmap attention only when it clears four tests.

1Repeated customer need
2Relevant segment and workflow
3Measurable outcome improvement
4Feasible and governable delivery

Anything else is a hypothesis to test, not a commitment to copy.

04
Solution exploration

Direction A fixes today's search. Direction B extends what search can understand.

They carry different value, risk and timing, but share the same data, instrumentation and relevance foundations.

Direction A

Strengthen the non-generative Solr experience.

Improve relevance, schema, metadata, facets, query handling and interface clarity in the system already powering search.

Best fit
Known-item lookup, exact fields, filtering, predictable enterprise workflows and permission-sensitive retrieval.
Value
Fastest route to broad improvements with lower delivery risk, explainable ranking and controlled operating cost.
Trade-off
Still depends on query vocabulary and metadata quality, so ambiguous or conceptual searches may remain difficult.
Relative profile
Low-to-medium cost and risk; measurable value can begin in 6-12 weeks after baseline work.
Direction B

Add semantic retrieval, then selective LLM experiences.

Use meaning-based retrieval for harder queries and add generated answers only where evidence shows they improve a real task.

Best fit
Exploration, vague intent, cross-content discovery and natural-language questions where users do not know exact terms.
Value
Recovers relevant items that lexical matching misses and can reduce the cognitive effort of complex discovery.
Trade-off
Raises data, evaluation, latency, cost, privacy and hallucination concerns, especially for generated summaries.
Relative profile
Medium-to-high cost and risk; prototypes can be quick, but trustworthy production value usually takes 3-6+ months.
Initial investment split
A/B70/30

Fund both in sequence, with a small parallel discovery track.

Put most capacity into Solr foundations while a bounded team validates semantic value on the hardest query set; shift investment only when the prototype beats lexical search and meets security, latency and cost gates.

Development

Prove feasibility and operating shape.

Run bounded spikes for schema, indexing, vector support, permissions, latency and cost before estimates become commitments.

Design

Prove comprehension and workflow fit.

Prototype both directions against the same customer tasks and test refinement, explanations, confidence and recovery.

Together

Judge evidence through one scorecard.

Review real queries, technical traces and observed task outcomes together, then recommend the next investment gate.

Hybrid search in simple language

AI adds context; Apache Solr remains the search engine.

Search execution, permissions, filtering and ranking stay inside Solr. A non-generative embedding model supplies numerical meaning, while an LLM is optional and downstream.

1. Prepare

Clean source data

Normalise titles, text, metadata, permissions and freshness signals.

2. Enrich

Add useful context

AI suggests tags, entities and summaries with confidence and governance controls.

3. Retrieve in Solr

Run two searches

Solr combines keyword ranking with dense-vector similarity under the same filters.

4. Blend

Rank the evidence

Weighted rules or reranking merge both result lists and preserve explainability.

5. Present

Show trusted results

Users see original sources first; a grounded answer layer can be tested later.

Important distinction

Semantic retrieval does not require a live generative LLM to write an answer. Embeddings represent meaning, while Solr retrieves and ranks the permitted source records.

05
Success measurement

Measure whether people complete the job, not whether they used the search box.

A shared scorecard links search quality to user behaviour, guardrails and business exposure.

01

Search task success

Percentage of search sessions that reach a defined downstream outcome without support or manual recovery.

ExampleA user searches for the Q3 campaign brief, opens the approved version and adds it to a campaign without asking Support.

02

Time to useful result

Median time from the first query to the first meaningful action, segmented by task and customer type.

ExampleA user submits a query and opens the correct approved asset 42 seconds later.

03

Failed-search rate

Zero-result, repeated reformulation and abandonment signals combined into a visible failure measure.

ExampleA search returns no results, the user tries two new queries, then leaves without opening an asset.

04

Relevance quality

NDCG@10 or reciprocal rank on a judged query set, with separate scores for lexical and semantic use cases.

ExampleFor "latest APAC product launch video," the approved video appears within the top three judged results.

05

Business exposure

Search-related tickets, support hours, account-health movement and renewal-risk mentions over time.

ExampleTrack whether accounts with high failed-search rates also create more tickets or mention findability during renewals.

Direction A proves reliability.

Expect lower zero-result and reformulation rates, better first-result relevance, faster task completion and fewer support contacts.

Direction B must prove incremental value.

Measure win rate on hard queries, grounded-answer accuracy, user preference, p95 latency and cost per successful task.

Response to the COO

This is not a promise of direct new revenue or two disconnected workstreams. It is a controlled investment in renewal protection, support efficiency and product adoption, with the semantic track funded only while it demonstrates incremental value over the repaired core.

06
Implementation considerations

Deliver value in gates, not one large search transformation.

Each phase produces customer value or evidence, and each gate can stop further investment.

Phase 0 | Weeks 0-4

Baseline and diagnose

Instrument the funnel, build a judged query set, interview users and audit Solr, schema, permissions and metadata.

Gate: a quantified problem by segment and task.
Phase 1 | Weeks 5-12

Repair Direction A

Tune relevance, improve indexing and query handling, expose useful facets and test interface changes with priority accounts.

Gate: measurable lift in task success and failure rate.
Phase 2 | Quarter 2

Prove semantic lift

Prototype embeddings and Solr vector retrieval on the hard-query set, shadow test it and run a limited customer beta.

Gate: incremental relevance within latency, cost and privacy limits.
Phase 3 | Quarter 3+

Scale hybrid selectively

Blend lexical and semantic retrieval, expand coverage and test a grounded answer layer only for validated workflows.

Gate: sustained customer value without trust regressions.

Data and platform

Metadata completeness, content extraction, Solr version and vector support, reindexing capacity and observability.

Security and governance

Permission filtering, tenant isolation, data residency, privacy review, model contracts and auditability.

Experience and adoption

Design research, result explanations, change management, Customer Success enablement and feedback capture.

AI-specific constraints

Embedding quality, model drift, hallucination risk, prompt injection, p95 latency and cost per successful query.

Commercial context

Renewal timing, customer commitments, contractual controls and the segments with the greatest value at risk.

Evaluation operations

Judged query ownership, experiment design, quality reviews and a durable process for relevance tuning.

07
Organisational leadership

Alignment comes from shared evidence, explicit decisions and predictable cadence.

The product leader owns the frame, the decision process and the connection between customer outcomes and investment.

Weekly

Delivery working group

Product, Engineering, Design, Data and Support review evidence, blockers, quality and experiment outcomes.

Monthly

Executive decision review

COO, VP Engineering, Finance, Sales and Customer Success review scorecard movement, risk and investment gates.

Quarterly

Customer advisory check

Priority accounts validate whether roadmap progress changes real workflows, trust and renewal confidence.

When senior stakeholders disagree

  1. Make the contested assumption explicit: customer value, feasibility, cost, risk or timing.
  2. Use the pre-agreed scorecard and decision gates, not role seniority, as the default arbitration mechanism.
  3. Run the smallest time-boxed experiment that can resolve the disagreement and record the decision.
  4. Commit to the chosen path until the next review trigger, then update openly when evidence changes.
Detailed evidence

The deeper reasoning behind the presentation.

Use these sections for questions, implementation discussion or follow-up reading. The overview above remains the primary pitch.

A1Problem framing, assumptions and portfolio decision

The decision protects near-term value while preserving an option on a materially better search experience. It avoids betting the full initiative on either a legacy-only path or an unproven generative layer.

Why not choose only Direction A?

Solr tuning can recover substantial value, but lexical relevance alone may not meet ambiguous, conceptual or natural-language discovery needs.

Why not lead with Direction B?

Semantic and generative experiences inherit the same metadata, permissions and evaluation problems; adding AI first can make an unreliable foundation harder to explain.

Assumptions to validate

  • Most search volume can improve through relevance, metadata and experience changes.
  • A smaller but valuable query set requires meaning-based retrieval.
  • The Solr estate can support, or be upgraded to support, dense-vector fields and kNN retrieval.
  • Permission rules can be applied consistently to lexical and vector candidates.
  • Search-related churn risk can be connected to observable customer behaviour.
  • Customers value source transparency more than answer-like novelty in high-stakes workflows.
A2Discovery plan, stakeholder sequence and business impact

Discovery combines behavioural data, account context and qualitative research. No single source can explain both the size of the problem and the reason users fail.

Weeks 1-2: map evidence

  • Audit events, logs and support taxonomy.
  • Sample zero-result, reformulated and abandoned queries.
  • Identify top-risk accounts, roles and workflows.
  • Create a judged query set with domain experts.

Weeks 2-3: observe users

  • Interview 8-12 users across enterprise and mid-market accounts.
  • Observe known-item, exploratory and analytic tasks.
  • Compare stated pain with actual behaviour.
  • Map workarounds, trust signals and consequences.

Weeks 3-4: align on scope

  • Size problems by segment, frequency and exposure.
  • Validate feasibility with Engineering and Design.
  • Agree baseline, targets and decision gates.
  • Present the evidence-led thesis to executives.
EvidenceWhat it revealsBusiness translation
Search tickets and handling timeRecurring defects, confused workflows and avoidable service demand.Ticket volume x average handling cost, plus escalations and account-management time.
Failed-search cohort behaviourWhether search failure predicts lower engagement or repeated support use.Compare retention and account-health movement with matched successful-search cohorts.
Renewal notes and risk flagsAccounts where search affects confidence or value perception.Sum contract value where search is a documented contributor, labelled revenue at risk rather than revenue lost.
Task time and workaroundsOperational effort hidden outside product analytics.Minutes lost x task frequency x affected users, used as a directional productivity estimate.

Stakeholder sequence

  1. Customer Success, Support and Analytics establish evidence.
  2. Customers and Design explain jobs, expectations and trust.
  3. Search Engineering, Data and Security define constraints.
  4. Sales and Renewals test commercial relevance and timing.
  5. Executives decide scope after the facts are visible.

Executive framing

Present a confidence range rather than false precision: search is a documented contributor to risk for defined accounts, creates measurable service cost and reduces successful product use.

A3Competitive benchmark method and relevance filter

Include 3 direct martech or digital-asset competitors, 2 established enterprise-search products and 2 AI-native search experiences. The goal is to learn how expectations are shifting, not to produce a feature inventory.

Run the same tasks everywhere

  • Find a known asset with incomplete naming.
  • Narrow results by campaign, date, region and rights.
  • Discover related content from a natural-language need.
  • Ask a cross-content question and verify each source.
  • Attempt a permission-sensitive task and observe safeguards.

Score evidence, not polish

  • Task completion and steps required.
  • Top-result relevance and recovery from weak queries.
  • Clarity of filters, ranking and explanations.
  • Latency, source transparency and permission behaviour.
  • Fit with segment frequency and consequence.
AreaKey questionEvidence of relevance
FindabilityDoes this improve high-frequency or high-consequence tasks?Observed success, query logs and repeated interview evidence.
AI capabilityDoes it solve an intent problem or only change the interface?Incremental win rate over repaired lexical search.
Trust and controlCan users verify, refine and safely act on the result?Source visibility, permissions, confidence and recovery behaviour.
Commercial valueWould target customers notice enough value to affect adoption or renewal confidence?Segment fit, account evidence and willingness to join a beta.
A4Direction comparison, hybrid architecture and AI principles
DimensionDirection A: Solr improvementDirection B: semantic and LLM experience
Core approachTune BM25 relevance, fields, analyzers, boosts, synonyms, spelling, schema, facets and interface behaviour.Add embeddings, dense-vector retrieval, hybrid ranking and optional retrieval-grounded answers.

Main benefitBroad, explainable improvement with faster time-to-value and lower operating risk.Better understanding of meaning when vocabulary does not match indexed text.
Main drawbackLimited semantic understanding and continued sensitivity to metadata quality.Higher evaluation, privacy, latency, cost and trust burden.
ValidationOffline relevance lift plus live task success and reduced failure behaviour.Incremental hard-query wins, groundedness, permission safety and acceptable economics.
Initial investment70% of capacity until core metrics stabilise.30% for data, prototype and validation; expand only through gates.

How semantic retrieval works

  1. Extract searchable text and approved metadata.
  2. Use an embedding model to create a dense vector representing meaning.
  3. Store vectors in Solr beside lexical fields, freshness and permissions.
  4. At query time, ask Solr for BM25 keyword and kNN vector candidates.
  5. Apply access filters, blend or rerank, then return original records with explanations.

How AI enriches context

  • Suggest missing tags, entities, themes, channels, regions and summaries.
  • Keep customer metadata authoritative and label machine suggestions.
  • Store confidence, model version and provenance for audit and rollback.
  • Send low-confidence or sensitive fields to human review.
  • Reprocess only when relevance gains justify the cost.

Direction A assumptions

Failures are materially driven by relevance configuration, schema, metadata and interaction design, and the current Solr estate can be improved without a disruptive rewrite.

Direction B assumptions

A valuable set of customer tasks depends on meaning rather than exact terms, and vector retrieval can outperform the repaired lexical baseline within governance and economic limits.

Development and Design

Engineering tests feasibility while Design tests task fit; both evaluate identical queries and prototypes so customer desirability and technical viability are decided together.

Retrieval is the control plane

Permissions, filters, freshness and ranking remain deterministic and testable in Solr.

Generation is optional

An LLM may summarise only permitted evidence for validated workflows; it never replaces source records.

Trust is a requirement

Show sources, communicate uncertainty and provide a clear path back to standard search.

A5Metric definitions, baseline and experiment design
MetricDefinitionWhy it matters
Search task successSuccessful downstream actions divided by eligible search sessions, defined by workflow.Connects search to completed work rather than clicks alone.
Time to useful resultMedian time from first query to the first verified useful action.Captures effort even when users eventually succeed.
Failed-search rateZero results, repeated reformulation or abandonment without a useful action.Shows friction that support tickets capture only after escalation.
NDCG@10 and MRROffline ranking quality on a query set judged by domain experts and customers.Allows safe iteration and separates lexical from semantic changes.
Business exposureSearch tickets per account, support hours, health delta and renewal-risk mentions.Explains investment without overstating direct revenue attribution.

Establish the baseline

  1. Define success events for the top 3-5 workflows.
  2. Collect at least four weeks of clean segmented data.
  3. Create a versioned query set from logs and interviews.
  4. Use multiple relevance judges to reduce individual bias.
  5. Set latency, cost, privacy and permission guardrails.

Track improvement

  1. Use offline evaluation for tuning and regression protection.
  2. Shadow-test semantic candidates before exposure.
  3. Run A/B or interleaving tests where traffic allows.
  4. Pair telemetry with customer task studies.
  5. Stop when a global average hides segment-level harm.

Illustrative gates to agree after baseline

  • Direction A: credible task-success lift with no permission or latency regression.
  • Direction B: clear win on the hard-query set beyond Direction A alone.
  • Generated answers: near-complete citation and zero tolerance for permission leakage.
  • Economics: cost per successful task inside an agreed envelope.
A6Rollout controls, technical risks and decision gates

Control the rollout

  • Start with shadow evaluation and internal users.
  • Use feature flags by account and content type.
  • Show a clear fallback to standard search.
  • Monitor failures, latency and permissions.
  • Predefine rollback triggers and ownership.

Protect search quality

  • Version schemas, embeddings and query sets.
  • Run regression tests on relevance changes.
  • Separate suggested from authored metadata.
  • Audit model drift and stale embeddings.
  • Treat relevance tuning as ongoing operations.

Protect trust and economics

  • Apply permissions before generation and display.
  • Use approved models and retention terms.
  • Cache only when access rules remain correct.
  • Track p95 latency and cost per successful task.
  • Do not scale features that cannot show sources.
RiskPotential harmMitigation
Metadata debtLexical and semantic results become noisy or stale.Quality scoring, provenance, ownership and targeted remediation.
Permission leakageUsers retrieve or receive summaries of inaccessible content.Tenant-aware indexing, filter-first retrieval and zero-tolerance gates.
Hallucinated answerA generated response invents or misstates information.Grounding, citations, constrained prompts, abstention and source-first design.
Latency and costBetter relevance creates a slower or uneconomic experience.Budgets, model selection, safe caching and feature-specific SLAs.
Change fatigueUsers distrust unfamiliar ranking or conversation.Progressive exposure, explanations, feedback and CS enablement.

One narrative for every audience

The initiative protects customer value today and builds evidence for tomorrow. The wording changes by stakeholder, but the scorecard and gates stay the same.

A living decision record

Record the question, evidence, owner, decision, dissent and review trigger. This prevents old debates restarting without new information.

Decision summary

Fix what is broken. Prove what is possible. Scale only what earns trust.

Keep Apache Solr as the governed retrieval core, improve the deterministic experience first, validate semantic lift on real customer tasks and reserve generative AI for grounded use cases where it adds measurable value.
